title: Endometriosis: Treat the Clinical Syndrome Without Waiting Years for Surgery
bottomLine: Endometriosis is a clinical syndrome of cyclic or persistent pelvic pain, dysmenorrhea, dyspareunia and sometimes infertility. Use history/exam and ultrasound for alternate/structural disease, begin evidence-based medical therapy when appropriate, and reserve surgery for specific diagnostic or therapeutic indications rather than requiring laparoscopy before treatment.
recognize: Pain severity may not match visible disease burden; bowel/bladder symptoms can be cyclic.
differentiate: Adenomyosis, fibroids, PID, IBS, pelvic floor myalgia and ovarian disease can overlap.
assessment: Assess pain pattern, bleeding, dyspareunia, bowel/bladder symptoms, fertility goals, prior therapy, mental health and functional impact.
workup: Pelvic ultrasound assesses endometrioma/structural disease but a normal scan does not exclude superficial endometriosis.
Use specialty imaging/surgery when deep disease, mass, organ involvement, infertility or refractory symptoms warrants it.
management: Offer NSAIDs and hormonal suppression appropriate to contraception/fertility goals and contraindications; refer persistent/refractory pain, endometrioma/deep disease or fertility concern.
medicationSafety: Hormonal therapy requires method-specific VTE/reproductive risk review; repeated opioids are not a disease-directed strategy.
redFlags: Acute severe pain with pregnancy possibility
counselling: Validate pain and explain that treatment can begin from a strong clinical diagnosis without forcing diagnostic surgery first.
followUp: Track function, bleeding, treatment adverse effects and fertility goals.
examTrap: Telling a patient endometriosis cannot be treated until laparoscopy proves it.
oneLinePearl: Endometriosis can be treated clinically; surgery is a tool, not a prerequisite for believing the pain.
sourceBasis: SOGC Guideline No. 449 Diagnosis and Impact of Endometriosis

title: Uterine Fibroids: Symptoms, Size, Location, and Fertility Goals Drive Care
bottomLine: Fibroids are common benign uterine tumors and are treated only when symptoms, anemia, pressure effects, fertility concerns or diagnostic uncertainty justify intervention. Ultrasound defines anatomy; treatment is individualized to bleeding, bulk symptoms, reproductive goals and proximity to menopause.
recognize: Heavy bleeding, pressure, urinary/bowel symptoms, enlarged irregular uterus and selected infertility patterns can occur.
differentiate: Adenomyosis, endometrial pathology, pregnancy and ovarian masses can mimic fibroid symptoms.
assessment: Assess bleeding burden/anemia symptoms, pressure/pain, fertility goals, pregnancy possibility and rapid/new postmenopausal growth concerns.
workup: Use pelvic ultrasound as first-line imaging and CBC/iron studies when bleeding is significant; endometrial evaluation follows AUB malignancy-risk criteria.
management: Options include observation, medical bleeding control, LNG-IUS where cavity anatomy permits, tranexamic acid/hormonal therapy and procedural/surgical options selected by goals/anatomy.
medicationSafety: Avoid assuming every fibroid is the bleeding source when endometrial malignancy risk requires assessment.
counselling: Explain that fibroid size alone does not mandate treatment and fertility-preserving options differ from definitive surgery.
followUp: Track symptoms/anemia rather than serial imaging of every stable asymptomatic fibroid.
examTrap: Treating an incidental asymptomatic fibroid or attributing all postmenopausal bleeding to known fibroids.
oneLinePearl: Treat fibroid symptoms and goals, not the ultrasound label alone.
sourceBasis: SOGC uterine leiomyoma and abnormal uterine bleeding guidance

title: PCOS: Reproductive, Metabolic, and Endometrial Risk in One Plan
bottomLine: PCOS is diagnosed from ovulatory dysfunction and hyperandrogenic/ovarian features after excluding important mimics. Management depends on goals for cycle/endometrial protection, contraception, fertility, hirsutism/acne and cardiometabolic risk—not on ovarian ultrasound alone.
recognize: Irregular cycles, clinical/biochemical hyperandrogenism and metabolic risk are common; polycystic ovarian morphology alone is not PCOS.
differentiate: Pregnancy, thyroid disease, hyperprolactinemia, nonclassic CAH and androgen-secreting tumors must be considered; rapid virilization is a red flag.
assessment: Assess menstrual pattern, androgen symptoms, fertility goals, eating/weight stigma, BP, diabetes risk, sleep apnea and mental health.
workup: Use pregnancy and targeted endocrine testing to exclude mimics; screen glycemia/lipids/BP based on current PCOS guidance.
management: Use lifestyle support without stigma, hormonal cycle protection/contraception when desired, metformin for appropriate metabolic/reproductive indications and ovulation induction through fertility pathways when needed.
medicationSafety: Avoid antiandrogen exposure in pregnancy; ensure reliable contraception when teratogenic antiandrogen therapy is used.
counselling: Explain that PCOS is a chronic reproductive-metabolic syndrome, not a diagnosis based on body size.
followUp: Track cycles/endometrial protection, metabolic risk and patient-defined symptom goals.
examTrap: Diagnosing PCOS from ultrasound alone or focusing only on fertility while ignoring endometrial/metabolic risk.
oneLinePearl: PCOS care protects cycles, metabolism and reproductive goals together.
sourceBasis: SOGC PCOS resources and 2025 position statement

title: Premature Ovarian Insufficiency: Confirm Hypoestrogenism and Protect Long-Term Health
bottomLine: POI is loss of ovarian function before the expected menopausal age and requires confirmation, cause-directed evaluation, pregnancy/fertility counselling and replacement of missing estrogen when not contraindicated to protect bone, cardiovascular and genitourinary health.
recognize: Amenorrhea/oligomenorrhea, vasomotor symptoms, infertility and low-estrogen symptoms can occur; intermittent ovulation is possible.
differentiate: Pregnancy, hypothalamic amenorrhea, PCOS, thyroid/prolactin disease and medication effects can mimic menstrual absence.
assessment: Assess menstrual history, pregnancy, vasomotor/genitourinary symptoms, surgery/chemo/radiation, autoimmune/genetic clues, fertility goals and eating/exercise context.
workup: Confirm persistent ovarian insufficiency with appropriate gonadotropin/estradiol testing and targeted thyroid/genetic/autoimmune evaluation when indicated.
management: Offer physiologic estrogen replacement with endometrial protection when uterus present and no contraindication, generally until usual menopausal age, plus bone/cardiovascular risk care and fertility referral if desired.
medicationSafety: POI hormone replacement is not the same risk-benefit context as initiating menopausal HT at older ages; contraindications still require individualized alternatives.
redFlags: Severe headache/visual symptoms suggesting pituitary disease
counselling: Discuss fertility uncertainty, emotional impact and spontaneous intermittent ovarian activity without promising pregnancy.
followUp: Monitor symptoms, adherence, bone/cardiovascular health and evolving fertility goals.
examTrap: Treating POI like ordinary menopause and withholding physiologic hormone replacement solely because of generalized fear of HT.
oneLinePearl: POI is early hormone deficiency with decades of health implications, not simply early hot flashes.

title: Menopause: Diagnose Clinically and Individualize Hormone Therapy
bottomLine: Menopause is usually a clinical diagnosis based on age, menstrual transition and symptoms, not routine FSH testing. Menopausal hormone therapy is the most effective treatment for vasomotor symptoms in appropriate patients; choose route, progestogen/endometrial protection and duration through individualized benefit-risk assessment.
recognize: Vasomotor symptoms, sleep disruption and genitourinary syndrome may occur before/after the final menstrual period.
differentiate: Thyroid disease, pregnancy and medication effects can mimic symptoms; postmenopausal bleeding always requires evaluation rather than being attributed to menopause.
assessment: Assess symptom burden, uterus status, bleeding, VTE/CVD/stroke, breast cancer, liver disease, migraine, smoking, bone risk and patient priorities.
workup: Routine hormone levels are unnecessary in typical-age menopause; targeted testing is used when age/pattern is atypical or another diagnosis is suspected.
management: Offer systemic MHT for appropriate bothersome vasomotor symptoms and local vaginal therapy for GSM when appropriate; use a progestogen to protect endometrium with systemic estrogen when uterus is present unless a validated alternative provides protection.
medicationSafety: Route/type matter for thrombotic/metabolic risk; unexplained vaginal bleeding, estrogen-dependent cancer and other major contraindications require evaluation/alternatives.
redFlags: Severe atypical symptoms requiring alternate diagnosis
counselling: Discuss absolute individualized benefits/risks rather than a universal maximum duration; revisit therapy as goals/risk change.
followUp: Review symptom control, bleeding, adverse effects and preventive health periodically.
examTrap: Ordering FSH to diagnose routine menopause or denying effective MHT solely because a fixed age/duration limit was memorized.
oneLinePearl: Menopause is usually clinical; hormone therapy is individualized, not one-size-fits-all.

title: Bone Health in Women: Prevent Fracture Across Reproductive and Menopausal Transitions
bottomLine: Bone prevention is fracture-risk prevention, not universal supplement prescribing. Identify premature estrogen loss, glucocorticoids, eating disorders, malabsorption, falls and menopausal fracture risk; use BMD/risk assessment when indicated and treat high fracture risk according to Osteoporosis Canada guidance.
recognize: POI/early menopause, prior fragility fracture and chronic glucocorticoids materially increase risk.
differentiate: Osteomalacia and secondary endocrine/renal bone disease require cause-specific treatment.
assessment: Assess fractures/falls, menopause timing, nutrition/eating disorder, medications, smoking/alcohol, activity and secondary-cause clues.
workup: Use age/risk-based BMD and targeted secondary-cause labs; avoid low-value vitamin D/BMD testing without indication.
management: Promote resistance/weight-bearing exercise, falls prevention and adequate calcium/vitamin D intake; use pharmacotherapy for risk-qualified patients and hormone replacement appropriately in POI.
medicationSafety: Avoid excessive calcium/vitamin D dosing and plan transitions for agents such as denosumab.
counselling: Focus on fracture prevention and strength/function rather than weight or supplement megadoses.
followUp: Reassess fractures/falls and treatment adherence; repeat BMD only when useful to management.
examTrap: Prescribing high-dose supplements to everyone while missing a fragility fracture or POI.
oneLinePearl: Women's bone care is risk, strength and fracture prevention—not supplement maximalism.

title: Breast Cancer: Separate Screening from Diagnostic Evaluation of a Symptom
bottomLine: Breast screening is for asymptomatic people and varies by provincial program and risk. A new breast mass, bloody nipple discharge, inflammatory skin change or suspicious node needs diagnostic imaging and tissue evaluation—not a routine screening mammogram referral.
recognize: Screening eligibility and intervals vary by province and individual risk; Ontario currently permits self-referral ages 40–74 for average-risk mammography.
differentiate: Screening mammography differs from diagnostic mammography/ultrasound for symptoms; high-risk hereditary pathways use different imaging schedules.
assessment: Ask mass duration/change, discharge, skin/nipple change, pregnancy/lactation, prior imaging/biopsy, family/genetic history and prior chest radiation.
workup: Use age/context-appropriate diagnostic ultrasound/mammography for a palpable abnormality and biopsy suspicious findings; do not reassure from a normal screening test when a clinically concerning mass persists.
management: Use the current provincial organized screening program for asymptomatic eligible patients and refer symptomatic/suspicious findings through diagnostic breast pathways.
medicationSafety: Avoid empiric antibiotics for a persistent breast mass unless infection is clinically supported; inflammatory breast cancer can mimic mastitis.
counselling: Explain benefits/harms of screening and that a symptom changes the type of test needed.
followUp: Track every abnormal imaging/biopsy recommendation to resolution.
examTrap: Sending a symptomatic breast mass through routine screening and considering the problem closed if the screening mammogram is normal.
oneLinePearl: Screen people without symptoms; diagnose breast symptoms.

title: Cervical Screening: HPV-Based Programs, Symptoms Stay Diagnostic
bottomLine: Cervical screening is for asymptomatic people with a cervix and increasingly uses primary HPV testing through provincial programs. A positive HPV screen is not cancer; follow the risk-based provincial algorithm. Unusual bleeding, postcoital bleeding or abnormal discharge requires diagnostic assessment rather than simply ordering the screening test.
recognize: Ontario's program moved to primary HPV screening in 2026, generally starting at 25 with longer intervals for HPV-negative average-risk patients.
Vaccination reduces risk but does not eliminate the need for screening in eligible people.
differentiate: Screening, surveillance after prior high-grade disease and diagnostic evaluation of symptoms are separate pathways.
assessment: Confirm cervix status, symptoms, prior HPV/cytology/colposcopy/treatment, immunocompromise, DES exposure where relevant and current provincial program.
workup: Use the current provincial HPV/cytology triage algorithm; refer high-risk results for colposcopy/treatment as indicated.
Do not use HPV testing as an STI screen unrelated to cervical screening indications.
management: Ensure abnormal screens reach definitive follow-up and surveillance after treatment follows the high-risk pathway.
medicationSafety: Avoid empiric treatment of HPV itself; management targets cervical precancer risk and associated lesions.
counselling: Explain that HPV may have been present for years and a positive result does not identify when/from whom infection came.
followUp: Use recall/tracking to ensure risk-based repeat testing or colposcopy occurs.
examTrap: Calling a positive HPV screen cervical cancer or using routine screening as the only response to postcoital bleeding.
oneLinePearl: HPV screening estimates cervical precancer risk; symptoms still need diagnosis.
sourceBasis: Ontario Health Cervical Screening Program HPV transition 2026

title: Endometrial Cancer: Postmenopausal Bleeding Is Cancer Until Evaluated
bottomLine: Postmenopausal bleeding requires endometrial evaluation because cancer must be excluded. Premenopausal abnormal bleeding also warrants sampling when age/risk/persistence raises concern. Ultrasound can stratify selected postmenopausal patients, but persistent/recurrent bleeding or abnormal findings require tissue diagnosis.
recognize: Postmenopausal bleeding is the classic warning symptom; obesity, chronic anovulation/PCOS, unopposed estrogen, tamoxifen and Lynch syndrome can increase risk.
differentiate: Atrophy is common but cannot be assumed before malignancy evaluation; cervical/vaginal lesions and medications are alternatives.
assessment: Confirm menopausal status, bleeding amount/recurrence, hormone/tamoxifen use, PCOS/anovulation, family history/Lynch risk and cervical/vaginal source.
workup: Use transvaginal ultrasound and/or endometrial sampling according to current provincial/gynecology pathways; persistent bleeding requires further evaluation even after an initially reassuring test when clinically indicated.
management: Refer confirmed/suspected malignancy to gynecologic oncology; stabilize heavy bleeding/anemia as needed.
medicationSafety: Do not prescribe estrogen for unexplained postmenopausal bleeding before evaluation.
counselling: Explain that most postmenopausal bleeding is not cancer but it must be checked promptly.
followUp: Track pathology/referral to definitive diagnosis and treatment.
examTrap: Reassuring postmenopausal bleeding as atrophy without completing endometrial evaluation.
oneLinePearl: Postmenopausal bleeding is a diagnostic problem, never a screening problem.
sourceBasis: Canadian gynecologic oncology and provincial endometrial-cancer diagnostic pathways
